name: Zinc

lead: Zinc is an essential mineral used as an oral supplement and in topical products, including zinc oxide sunscreens and acne formulations. People use it for inflammatory acne and for hair shedding associated with deficiency.
Benefits are most convincing when actual deficiency is corrected; in zinc-replete people, evidence for improved acne or appearance is limited.

paras: Zinc supports enzyme function, wound healing, immune regulation and keratinocyte biology, and it has mild anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects that are thought to relate to acne improvement.
High-dose supplementation can cause nausea and, over time, copper deficiency. Intake above requirements has not been shown to offer additional benefit. Zinc is available without prescription.

lead: Zinc is an essential trace element in humans, a cofactor for many enzymes (Grokipedia puts the number above 300) and the second most abundant trace metal in the body after iron [1][2]. In appearance and skin contexts it is taken as an oral supplement and applied topically, for example in zinc oxide products and acne formulations, and it is discussed for inflammatory acne and for hair shedding linked to deficiency [3][4].

A 2020 systematic review and meta-analysis found that people with acne had lower serum zinc than controls and that zinc treatment, as monotherapy or adjunct, was associated with a significant improvement in inflammatory papule counts, without a significant difference in side effects versus comparators; the authors noted that definitive evidence of efficacy had been lacking [3]. Wikipedia states that excess zinc intake may cause ataxia and lethargy, among other effects, and that deficiency affects roughly two billion people in the developing world [1].
infobox: Essential trace mineral (element Zn, atomic number 30) [1]
Oral supplement, diet; topical (zinc oxide, other salts)
11 mg (adult men), 8 mg (adult women) per day, per Grokipedia [2]
Zinc sulfate, acetate, gluconate, citrate, oxide [22][23]
Dietary supplement; zinc oxide is an active ingredient in OTC skin protectants [6]

paras: Zinc is used orally and topically for inflammatory acne, with proposed anti-inflammatory and antibacterial effects [3]. A 2024 review of zinc, copper and iron in selected skin diseases discusses the minerals' roles in skin conditions [5]. Zinc oxide is a skin-protectant ingredient; a US drug label for a zinc oxide diaper cream lists indications to help prevent and treat diaper rash and to protect chafed skin, with warnings for external use only and to avoid contact with eyes [6]. Hair shedding associated with zinc deficiency is described in clinical discussion of the mineral, with benefit generally expected when a deficiency exists [5][4].

A 2024 systematic review of 38 randomised trials, commissioned by the WHO for revision of its guidelines, examined zinc for acute and persistent diarrhoea in children [7]. Zinc has also been studied for pneumonia in children, immune function, pressure ulcers, oral mucositis and other conditions [8][9][10][11].

Acne: the 2020 meta-analysis reported significantly lower serum zinc in acne patients and an improvement in inflammatory papule counts with zinc treatment, with no significant difference in side-effect incidence [3]. An early controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris was published in 1978 [12].

Other areas: a Cochrane review of nutritional interventions for pressure ulcers (2024) is among the wound-related syntheses [9]; a randomised trial tested zinc chloride mouthwash for chemotherapy-related oral mucositis [10]; and a 2025 randomised trial tested zinc as adjuvant treatment in SARS-CoV-2 [13]. A 2024 crossover trial reported improved absorption of a glycoprotein matrix zinc form [14]. Registered trials include absorption studies of zinc citrate, gluconate and oxide, childhood pneumonia (641 participants) and a large 2026 trial of zinc and infections in older medical patients [15][16][17]. A 2017 review describes zinc as a gatekeeper of immune function [18].

Wikipedia notes that consumption of excess zinc may cause ataxia and lethargy, among other effects [1]. Grokipedia describes zinc as non-toxic at typical dietary levels and notes that inhaling zinc oxide dust can cause metal fume fever [2]. The 2020 acne meta-analysis found no significant difference in side-effect incidence between zinc and comparators [3].

Zinc is the only metal found in all enzyme classes, is required for prenatal and postnatal development, and deficiency in children is linked to growth retardation, delayed sexual maturation, infection susceptibility and diarrhoea [1]. A 2024 review covers its role in health and disease, including immune regulation and wound healing [4][18]. Absorption differs between forms, which has been compared in small bioavailability trials [14][15].

Zinc ores were used to make brass long before the metal was identified; metallic zinc was isolated in India by about 1300 and the name zincum is credited to Paracelsus in the 16th century [1]. Its recognition as an essential nutrient and its use in dermatology are more recent; zinc sulfate was trialled for acne in 1978 [12].

lore.intro: On looksmax.org zinc is discussed as a routine supplement, often taken with other compounds such as GHK-Cu, with threads on dosage, forms, effects on the voice and what to do after taking too much [19][20][21].

claims.claim: Zinc should be supplemented at around 30 to 50 mg per day while using GHK-Cu.
Zinc made a user's voice deeper.
Excess zinc intake requires copper supplementation afterwards.

timeline.event: Metallic zinc is isolated in India, per Wikipedia [1].
Controlled trial of zinc sulfate in acne vulgaris is published [12].
Meta-analysis reports lower serum zinc in acne and improved inflammatory papule counts with zinc [3].
